issues.what_breaks: The analyst recommends constructive because the agreement registry shows ≥60% Tier 1/2 coverage and ≥40% year-two, and the stock rises initially. But the agreements represent customers pulling forward, not incremental volume, so revenue growth in years 2–3 reverts to baseline trend. The analyst realizes in year 3 that the hypothesis was wrong, but by then the thesis has been tested.
issues.fix: State a specific falsifier: 'The hypothesis predicts that committed volume increases revenue run-rate by ≥15% on a 3-year forward basis (year 2–3 average vs. company and industry growth trend). If realized revenue growth in years 2–3 is within 5pp of the pre-shortage growth trend (i.e., indistinguishable from extrapolation), the mechanism did not work and the position is exited.' Or: 'The hypothesis predicts that customer revenue per dollar of agreement value is ≥80% of the announced value within 24 months of agreement signing (accounting for ramps). If realized is <60%, the agreements were overvalued and we liquidate.' Pre-commit to one such test and check it in year 2 post-entry.

issues.summary: The plan does not consider the null hypothesis or the other side of the trade — why would the market be wrong about the durability of these agreements, and who is short or underweighting that assumes they are not durable?
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan builds a case for why the stock should re-rate based on durable revenue. But it does not articulate the bull and bear cases side-by-side. Why might the agreements NOT reduce variance or extend horizon? (a) Renegotiation pressure — once the shortage is over, customers leverage countervailing power and amend terms, reducing the durability; (b) competition — new entrants or substitutes emerge, and customers shift suppliers within the agreement window; (c) optionality — the agreement contains favorable renegotiation clauses for the customer (e.g., pricing adjustment clauses if commodity costs fall), limiting locked-in margin; (d) demand destruction — the shortage induced hoarding; true underlying demand is flat or declining; (e) obsolescence — the product category is disrupted mid-agreement (e.g., old-tech passes to new tech, and the agreement is for the old technology). None of these are modeled. The plan assumes the agreements are quasi-debt and will perform, but concentrated fund managers know that industrial agreements are renegotiated when conditions change. If the analyst has not thought through the other side, the due diligence is incomplete.
issues.what_breaks: The analyst recommends constructive based on Tier 1/2 coverage and the model seems airtight. The stock rallies. Two years later, two of the top-3 customers renegotiate pricing down due to cost pressure and slowing demand, and revenue growth falls short of model. The PM asks: did we consider renegotiation risk? The analyst says 'we thought the agreements were binding,' and the PM knows that was naive — most industrial agreements have escape clauses or renegotiation norms.
issues.fix: Before delivering the recommendation, have the analyst write a one-page 'bull and bear' summary: (a) bull: agreements are genuine, binding (take-or-pay enforced, cash received), and customers are locked in for X years at pricing that reflects current scarcity; (b) bear: renegotiation is likely if (i) commodity costs fall >15%, (ii) customer financial distress emerges, or (iii) product substitutes are available; agreements are binding in law but weak in practice; (c) mitigants: which agreements have the strongest cash support, which customers have the least leverage, which products have the fewest substitutes?; (d) false positive risk: if the agreements are locked but underlying demand is soft, durability is real but growth is not, and the stock re-rates down on lower-than-expected volume ramp (not margin compression). Require the analyst to articulate the case that would prove the thesis wrong and state why that case is unlikely before delivering a constructive call.

issues.summary: The plan compares EV/haircut-adjusted committed gross profit to peers and prior periods, but does not specify what peers (by product, by region, by maturity stage?) and does not state whether the current multiple is already extended relative to history.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan states: 'Compare EV/haircut-adjusted committed gross profit (normalized margin) across time and peers.' This is a valuation step, but it lacks anchors. Which peers? If the company is a diversified supplier, different product lines trade at different multiples (high-margin IP at premium multiples, commodity components at discount). Comparing the company's EV/adjusted gross profit to peers' EV/reported gross profit is mixing. Also, comparing to 'prior periods' requires defining 'normal.' If the stock has risen 50% in the past 6 months due to the shortage guidance, the current multiple might already be extended, and finding that the model implies additional durability does not mean the stock is cheap — it means the shortage priced some durability already. Without a baseline (what was the multiple one year ago, what do sell-side consensus earnings imply about priced-in durability), the valuation step is incomplete.
issues.what_breaks: The analyst calculates EV / (haircut-adjusted committed gross profit) = 18x and says this is in-line with peer average of 18x, so the stock is fairly valued but should re-rate higher if the durability thesis is right. But the analyst did not check whether the stock's multiple has expanded from 14x (one year ago) to 18x due to the shortage guidance already pricing some durability. The analyst's conclusion that 'the stock should re-rate higher' is based on the faulty premise that the current multiple does not reflect the coverage expansion.
issues.fix: Before calculating valuation impact, state: (a) the historical multiple (EV/NTM reported gross profit) one year ago, 6 months ago, now; (b) the consensus multiple (what implied durability or margin do consensus earnings imply?); (c) the peer comparable (EV/gross-profit for peers with similar product mix, not all peers); (d) the gap the model fills (if the model implies 2 years more durability than consensus, what is that worth in EV/gross-profit multiple terms?). Then: current multiple is X, model implies Y, gap is Z, which is the actionable insight.

issues.summary: The plan names six-attribute scoring of agreements (minimums, pricing, cash, take-or-pay %, cancellation, RPO inclusion) but does not provide a scoring rubric or formula — the weights and decision rules are left to analyst judgment, making replication impossible.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The tiering logic (Tier 1: 90–95%, Tier 2: 70%, Tier 3: 25–35%) is supposed to be derived from the six attributes, but the plan does not state the rule. Does an agreement need all six attributes to be Tier 1, or just cash + take-or-pay? If an agreement has cash + take-or-pay + RPO inclusion but cancelable terms, is it Tier 1 or Tier 2? If it has minimums + pricing fixed + RPO but no cash and no take-or-pay, what tier? The plan leaves this to analyst judgment. In a fund review, when the PM asks why $200M of revenue is Tier 1 and not Tier 2, the analyst will have to defend judgment calls. If a second analyst audits the tier assignments, they will disagree.
issues.what_breaks: The analyst assigns $2B of agreement value across tiers. An auditor spot-checks three large agreements and finds: Agreement A ($300M, minimums + fixed pricing + RPO + 25% take-or-pay, no cash) is Tier 1; Agreement B ($250M, minimums + fixed pricing + RPO + no take-or-pay, $50M upfront cash) is Tier 2. Why is the tier designation different if the second agreement has more cash? The analyst's answer is 'Agreement A has take-or-pay and agreement B does not,' but the plan does not make clear whether take-or-pay is the dominant signal or equally weighted with cash. The tier assignments lack defensibility.
issues.fix: Provide a scoring rubric: (a) define each attribute on a 0–100 scale (e.g., minimum commitments: 0 = best-efforts only, 50 = soft minimums, 100 = hard minimums with ramp); (b) state the tier formula (e.g., Tier 1: minimum + pricing + take-or-pay + RPO all ≥75, OR cash ≥20% of value; Tier 2: minimum + pricing ≥75 but take-or-pay <75, OR cash 10–20%; Tier 3: everything else); (c) apply the rubric to every material agreement (>$10M) in a matrix the PM can see and audit; (d) test inter-rater reliability by having the analyst score three test agreements and then having a second person (PM or external auditor) score them independently and compare. Disagreements trigger a rubric clarification.

response.overall: This is a sophisticated research plan written for a data engineering and quant research firm, not a five-person fundamental long-only manager. The core idea is sound — shortages that induce binding, cash-backed agreements can durably extend revenue and reduce variance — but the execution plan is over-scoped and undefensible to the firm's audience. The agreement-registry tiering model requires ongoing infrastructure the firm cannot maintain, the six-attribute scoring lacks a defensible rubric, and the time and effort burn (5–6 weeks for one analyst) is unjustified without early kill gates. Most critically, the plan measures a gross-profit durable horizon but does not model the earnings and FCF conversion, so a 'constructive' recommendation on durable gross profit can easily fail on net income. The firm should either (a) radically simplify to RPO trending and peer-multiple comparison only, a two-week project that can be audited; (b) partner with a vendor that maintains agreement registries and tier them; or (c) kill the project and use that analyst-time elsewhere. As written, it will consume weeks, produce a complex recommendation the PM cannot defend internally, and likely fail to predict stock performance because it is missing earnings-level detail. Recommend a redesign with early kill gates (week 1), simplified inputs (disclosed LTA only), and a lower evidence bar calibrated to Type I risk.

issue_buckets.why: Not in gold, but a serious and plan-specific objection for this desk: quarterly maintenance of an LTA register assembled from 8-Ks, IR decks, customer press releases and customers' own purchase-obligation tables, plus cross-supplier and mirror-disclosure reconciliation, is an infrastructure task at a five-person shop with no engineers, and a six-attribute judgment score is hard to make inspectable for a skeptical IC. Grounded in the actual mechanics of this plan, not a generic complaint.

Not gold. Legitimate for a 25-30 name book: the plan's six conditions are binary entry gates with no mapping from marginal/partial evidence to conviction or position size, and no rule for the near-miss case. Tied to the plan's specific thresholds rather than recited in the abstract.

Partially earned: the plan stops at haircut-adjusted committed gross profit and names the capex/depreciation margin-trough as a risk without quantifying it or carrying it to FCF, leverage or EPS. But the plan does include the depreciation schedule against 3-year agreements and a reverse DCF, so the gap is narrower than claimed; borderline between a real modelling hole and an over-read.

Legitimate in substance for this firm (no process for surfacing amendments, attributing LTA-to-RPO gaps, restating definition changes, or QC of tier assignments by a second person), and the contingent-LTA-tied-to-customer-capex example is plan-specific. Heavily overlaps [0], and 'no workflow specified' is the kind of complaint that would land against most research plans, hence uncertain.

Same concern as gold blocking#3 (haircuts calibrated off the single 2021-23 semiconductor episode, questionable transfer to a different industry) and gold secondary#2 (the 90-95/70/25-35 tiers asserted rather than derived, no sensitivity).

Not gold, and specific rather than canonical: it catches that the double-ordering guard requires competing-suppliers' backlog and independent unit forecasts that appear nowhere in the data-required list, that a quarterly point-in-time register cannot detect post-signature amendments, and that reflexivity is named but never tested (e.g. share of committed value signed in the guidance quarter). A desk would take these seriously.

Not gold (gold#2 is about the thresholds being underived; this is about their operation). Legitimate: 'negative on any of' plus bright lines like >1.5x channel inventory with no monitoring cadence, no partial-breach escalation and no rule for one vs two quarters leaves the exit discipline decided after the fact on a concentrated position.

Not gold. Real for a two-analyst shop: the plan is a single long pipeline with no cheap feasibility gate (e.g. does this company still disclose LTA values and ship schedules at all?) before weeks of register construction, and a 'negative' verdict yields no reusable output.

Not gold. Earned and specific: the reverse DCF is the plan's central test of 'EV does not already price it', yet the market-implied horizon has no stated anchor (consensus vs guidance vs the analyst's own base case, which is circular) and no discount-rate/terminal assumptions, so the ≥2-year horizon gap is not measurable as specified.

Not gold. Legitimate: 'normalized margin' is the valuation denominator and is left undefined, and the plan's own three resolution scenarios imply different pricing/margin paths (early rolloff, late extension) that a single flat normalized margin would suppress.

The segment-aggregation point is a genuine bite (consolidated inventory will mask a single bottleneck line, and the plan's coherence check assumes disaggregation that filings often do not provide). Weakened by the DSO digression, which mostly restates the plan's intended use of the signal, so partly a quibble.

Same family as gold blocking#3: the calibration/validation evidence base is too thin and selected to support the inferred conversion rates. Adds selection-logic and false-positive-rate framing, but the core objection is the reviewer's insufficient-base-rate point.
Legitimate opportunity-cost point for a five-person shop, but essentially a restatement of [7] (no intermediate gate, effort not recoverable), so it adds little independent content.

Not gold and genuinely sharp: all six gates can pass while the hypothesis (variance reduction and horizon extension) is false because the commitments are pull-forward of existing demand rather than incremental, and the evaluator proposes a concrete falsifier (de-trended year-two revenue per customer). The plan's duration/level pitfall gestures at this but does not test it.

Recites the canonical 'no bear case / agreements get renegotiated' objection against a plan whose stated prior is that enforceable cash-backed commitment 'is usually weak', that names enforcement/renegotiation as the likely outcome absent cash, that haircuts non-RPO commitments to 25-35% and near zero in a downturn, that scores indexed/renegotiable pricing explicitly, and that includes double-ordering/hoarding checks. The characterisation that the plan 'assumes the agreements are quasi-debt and will perform' misreads the plan; the justification would read identically against any commitment-analysis plan.

Its central complaint - that the analyst may not check whether the multiple already embeds the durability - is what the plan's stated hypothesis ('current EV does not already price that'), its across-time multiple comparison, and its reverse DCF for market-implied horizon exist to do. The peer-comparability point (adjusted vs reported gross profit, mixed product-line multiples) is a fair but thin residue, hence uncertain.

Same concern as gold secondary#2: the tiering apparatus is asserted rather than derived - here the missing rule mapping the six attributes to Tier 1/2/3 and their relative weights, which makes the tier assignments and their haircuts indefensible in an IC review.

response.plan_implied_asker: Systematic cross-sectional researcher with large multi-asset infrastructure and legal discovery resources
response.what_would_falsify: Episodes where contracted price stayed materially above spot for 8+ quarters post-normalization, absent a hard qualification moat; pre-registered checks on HBM case within 12 months. However, the definition of 'materially above' and the method for isolating price from volume in mixed settlements is not pre-committed.

issues.summary: The plan is architected for a firm with legal discovery, systematic data infrastructure, and researchers who can maintain a cross-market database. Your shop has neither.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The centerpiece is building a capacity ledger per market, coding 20-30 contracts from PACER/foreign courts, reconciling supplier/customer/shipment data, tracking SEMI qualifications, and integrating 6+ commodity price feeds. One analyst executing this serially with Excel and manual lookups will spend 6+ months on data assembly before any analysis. The firm cannot staff a legal researcher, maintain a consolidated market database, or license the specialized price feeds (TrendForce, Fastmarkets, UxC, Xeneta) at scale. This is a quant-shop plan, not a fundamental shop plan.
issues.what_breaks: If you attempt it: months sink into data before you know whether the core claim holds. If you skip it: you are spot-checking without the systematic grounding that makes the variance claims credible. Either way, the IC watches an analyst disappear into a spreadsheet for half a year.
issues.fix: Pivot to a single well-understood market with public price/volume history and clear contract disclosure (auto semi 2021-2025, or HBM holdout alone). Use only supplier 10-Ks, customer purchase-obligation tables (Item 7), and published price series. Abandon the capacity ledger and legal database; those are infrastructure plays.

issues.summary: The plan asks for evidence a concentrated fundamental shop cannot produce: consistent ordering by qualification-lag rank across 20-30 episodes, each drawn from a different market, each with non-comparable contract semantics.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan requires 20-30 matched episodes to validate that qualification lag is the structural variable. A concentrated manager has 25-30 names total. Your IC will see 20-30 different supplier-customer pairs, from polysilicon to containers to HBM, and reasonably ask: why should a pattern in polysilicon in 2009 predict HBM in 2026? Each episode requires contract coding on a hidden-variable (qualification-lag) whose ground truth is inaccessible — nobody discloses requalification cost or lag directly, so the coder infers it from industry lore. One analyst coding 30 episodes for a hidden variable, with no standardized source and no blind review, will not survive an IC challenge. A pattern order that holds across five random episodes is noise; across 30 coded by the same researcher under selection pressure is overfitting.
issues.what_breaks: You build a ranking that looks ordinal and systematic. The IC asks why polysilicon should predict lithium, and whether qualification lag is really the variable or a post-hoc story. You cannot answer without invoking domain expertise you have not documented. The ranking collapses in any new episode.
issues.fix: Narrow to one or two matched markets with clear institutional parallels (auto semis vs. HBM, both with publicly-disclosed mid-program qualification locks, both with defined-term capacity expansions tied to the SPA). Validate the ranking within that narrow set, present it as conditional on structural similarity, and state that generalization to other markets is not supported. Or: do not rank by hypothesis at all; instead, report the rate of price recovery to spot by market and let the IC see which were exceptions and why, without claiming a unified rule.

issues.summary: The plan measures whether LTAs 'break in price' and 'hold in volume,' but the data mixes three different outcomes (price-down renegotiation, walk, prepayment recovery) that your supply-demand analysis cannot distinguish and your customer disclosures will not decompose.
issues.why_it_applies_here: When a customer 'walks' from a contract (ocean containers, some semis), they took a legal hit and spot was cheaper; the plan counts it as 'price broken.' When a supplier reprices mid-term via reopener or prepayment refund (LNG SPAs, some polysilicon), both sides claim compliance; the plan must infer the true price. When shipment stays contractual but invoice is renegotiated off the books (common in B2B, never disclosed), your ASC 606 RPO will show no breakage and your customs data will show normal volume. The ordinal scale (durable/repriced/walked) requires three-way decomposition that your public data does not support. A customer 10-K says 'purchase obligations of $X' but does not disclose which of those $X were repriced, which were walked, which were executed at original price. You will infer this from capacity/price/shipment data and be right 70% of the time.
issues.what_breaks: You code 20 episodes, assign 15 to 'repriced' and 5 to 'held,' and rank by qualification lag. The ranking appears to hold. Your IC asks: how do you know Infineon customers truly renegotiated if Infineon's 10-K still lists the obligation? Your answer: 'I inferred it from the gap between capacity additions and backlog.' That is not evidence; it is a story overlaid on sparse data. When you live-test on HBM (where you promised to track repricing within 12 months), you find that the contract-liability number moved (suggesting repricing) but customer purchase-obligation tables did not (suggesting it did not). Which is correct? You cannot tell without the contract, which you do not have.
issues.fix: Acknowledge that only episodes where repricing is public (Hemlock litigation, China semi deposit refunds, LNG reopeners in foreign court records) are directly observable; for the rest, classify as 'outcome indeterminate.' Report only on the subset where the data directly resolves the question. For the live HBM test, get explicit sign-off on what counts as breach evidence before Jan 2025, and commit to a single source (customer 10-K obligation table, yes-or-no increase year-on-year) rather than triangulating across three sources.

issues.summary: The plan attempts to isolate price from volume in a setting where they are mechanically entangled and suppliers will not separate them.
issues.why_it_applies_here: When customers repriced semis mid-LTA, they did so by accepting lower allocation percentages at original price, or original allocation at lower price, or some combination opaque to public filings. Your ASC 606 revenue disclosures and customs data will show the realized quantity and your price feeds show spot, but you cannot back out the actual deal terms from that gap. The 'customer breach arithmetic' (spot savings vs. penalty PV, assuming suppliers preemptively concede) is not testable from public data. A supplier's 10-K may show contract-liability write-down, but that tells you money moved, not whether the customer got spot-price terms. You will infer it from the size of the write-down and the supplier's margin — reasonable, but a story, not data. When your HBM pre-register calls for tracking 'customer 10-K obligation table increase,' you are betting that LTA unwind will show up as a reported reduction. If the unwound volume is simply rebooked at lower price in the same line item, the obligation table grows numerically but the unit price falls silently. Your check fails because price and volume are not separable in the disclosure.
issues.what_breaks: You code polysilicon as 'repriced 85-90% of volume to spot within 3 years' based on supplier margin compression and contract-liability write-down timing. You present this as a robust finding. Your IC asks: did customers really get spot price, or did suppliers concede volume (sell less at original price) and call it a loss? You answer: 'margin compression implies price, not volume.' That is the inverse error — margin falls if suppliers cut price *or* if they cut volume and fixed costs don't move proportionally. You have not separated the two.
issues.fix: For polysilicon, mining (Hemlock litigation, court filings, settlement terms) gives you actual prices. For semis, customer disclosure (TSMC, Samsung customer concentration tables, industry reports) may show repricing where a contract reprices downward visibly. For everything else, admit the data does not separate price and volume recovery and report only rate of nominal contract-liability reduction, not its composition. Drop the price-vs-volume split as a finding; it is what you are trying to infer, not what you observe.

issues.summary: The plan proposes building a capacity ledger and predicting which suppliers have 'hidden capacity' — a Hidden variable you cannot observe — as the key predictor of price hold.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You write: 'capacity ledger per market (additions, ramp curves, hidden capacity) for the gap between supply-demand balance and weighted-average LTA maturity — the key predictor.' Hidden capacity is capacity you infer from the gap between announced supply balance and actual price behavior. This is circular: you observe price did not fall as much as announced capacity would predict, infer there must be hidden capacity, then use inferred hidden capacity to predict price does not fall. A supplier with spare capacity has incentive not to disclose it (keeps customers in long-term agreements rather than spot); a supplier in true shortage will not lie to Wall Street about capacity and face SEC enforcement; so hidden capacity *might* exist. But you cannot detect it from public data without already knowing whether price held. If price held and capacity balanced as announced, you infer hidden capacity. If price fell, you infer announced capacity was correct. The framework explains every outcome and predicts none.
issues.what_breaks: You apply this to HBM and predict: SK Hynix and Samsung will maintain contracted prices on 8-9 quarters post-normalization because 'hidden capacity is low.' When (if) they do, you report success. When (if) they don't, you report 'hidden capacity was higher than expected' or 'qualification lag was shorter.' The framework does not falsify.
issues.fix: Drop hidden capacity as an inferred variable. Instead, rank only on disclosed factors: announced capex, guidance, confirmed customer mix (customer disclosure), qualification timeline from public sources (roadmaps, SEMI reports). If the announced supply adds up to overhang but price does not fall, that is data you do not explain — report it as falsifying the price-floor model, not as evidence of hidden capacity. Admit you cannot detect hidden capacity from public data and stop trying.

issues.summary: The plan assigns falsifiability to a criterion ('price stayed above spot 8+ quarters absent qualification moat') but does not pre-commit to the definitions of 'materially above,' 'spot,' or 'qualification moat' that will be tested against HBM.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You write: 'Falsifier: episodes where contracted price stayed materially above spot for 8+ quarters post-normalization, absent a hard qualification moat.' On HBM, you plan to check this within 12 months via 'customer 10-K obligation table increase' and 'customs shipment tracking.' The problem: (a) you have not defined what counts as 'materially above' — is 2% above spot a hold or a repricing? At what threshold do you declare falsification? (b) 'Spot' has no single number for HBM — spot is a range (negotiated bid/ask spread); you will choose the number that best fits your thesis; (c) 'hard qualification moat' is not testable from public data — you infer it from end-market (aerospace semis are harder to requalify than memory). When HBM price data lands in 12 months, you will have three sliders (definition of materially, choice of spot reference, strictness of moat threshold) that let you rationalize any outcome as consistent with the framework.
issues.what_breaks: HBM price data arrives Q4 2024 / Q1 2025. Spot HBM price averaged $12-18/GB; some LTA references were $8-14/GB; some shipments happened at $15/GB. Did price 'materially' hold above spot? You have three different spot numbers and no pre-committed threshold. You rationalize it as success either way.
issues.fix: Before any HBM data lands, publish a memo stating: (1) the specific price benchmarks you will use (TrendForce spot index, CCMP bid/ask, or a named third-party source), (2) the minimum dollar-per-unit gap that counts as 'material' (e.g., $2/GB or 15% above spot), (3) the specific customer 10-K line item you will monitor, and (4) the specific check you will run. Commit to that memo. Or: abandon the live HBM test and confine the analysis to historical episodes where price recovery is documented (polysilicon, containers), not where you must infer it.

issues.summary: The plan lays out a method so data-intensive and technically intricate that a PM or IC member cannot evaluate it, and your firm has no one who can maintain or defend it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan requires: (1) legal document retrieval from PACER and foreign jurisdictions, (2) contract coding on semantic categories that vary by region and counterparty, (3) custom capacity databases merged with guidance and capex, (4) six external data feeds (TrendForce, Fastmarkets, UxC, Xeneta, Drewry, Panjiva), (5) regression-free ranking logic that is harder to explain than regression, (6) reconciliation of three data sources where they disagree. An IC member reading this will ask: how do I know the contract coding is right? How do I verify the capacity ledger? What happens if TrendForce's 'spot' price diverges from Fastmarkets'? Do we license these feeds permanently or run the whole thing once? One analyst executing this alone cannot document it well enough for the next analyst or PM to take over. If your analyst leaves, the code and the data structure vanish. If the market moves fast, the data is stale before the analysis is done.
issues.what_breaks: You spend 4 months building the framework and running the analysis on polysilicon + semis + memory. The conclusion is 'LTA durability depends on qualification lag, and HBM is a holdout case.' Your IC buys it. Then your analyst leaves, or HBM prices drop and a customer calls with a question, or you want to add lithium to the analysis. You have no documentation for the capacity ledger, no version control on the contract coding, no code to re-run it. You have a binder of spreadsheets. The edge was in the analyst's head.
issues.fix: Do not build a portable analytical system. Write a single-name memo on one cycle (auto semis 2021-2025, or HBM alone) that your PM can read and an IC can audit. Use only sources a PM would consult anyway (10-K, earnings calls, published price histories, industry reports). Avoid custom databases. The output should be narrative with data tables, not a framework for scaling to 20 markets.

issues.summary: The plan proposes holding out the auto-semis 2021-2024 cycle for validation, but that cycle is already complete and closing, making it unclear whether you are back-testing or validating.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You write: 'Validation: hold out the 2021-2024 auto-semi cycle, build the framework on the rest, predict holdout outcomes with dates before checking.' But you wrote this plan in late 2024, at the end of that very cycle. The 2021-2024 auto-semi LTA repricing is largely done; the data is not hidden, it is in historical 10-Ks. When you 'predict holdout outcomes with dates before checking,' you will see whether your model's dates match when repricing was announced, but the repricing itself is already visible in prior disclosures. This is not validation, it is back-fitting a model to available data and testing it on data that shares the same source. If your model predicts 'auto semis repriced 3-4 quarters into the cycle' and the 10-Ks show repricing was announced 3-4 quarters in, you have confirmed your read of public documents, not predicted a hidden pattern.
issues.what_breaks: Your IC asks: is the model predicting the repricing, or are you reading the dates from the 10-Ks and working backward? You answer: 'I built the model on polysilicon and memory, then predicted auto semis.' But you chose polysilicon and memory because they are fully resolved, removing selection pressure. The model was fit to find a lag-based pattern; auto semis are tested on the same type of data (10-K disclosures) that taught the pattern. This is not out-of-time validation.
issues.fix: Narrow validation to HBM (not yet resolved, truly live) and do not use the auto-semis holdout as validation. Or: use auto semis purely to build the hypothesis and commit to validating on HBM, without claiming you 'predicted' the auto semis cycle.

issues.summary: The plan ranks episodes by a variable (qualification-lag) that has no standard definition, and the ranking is done by a single researcher without blind review or inter-coder check.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Qualification lag (time to retool and validate a new supplier in a customer's process) is not disclosed. You infer it from industry knowledge (aerospace programs are 18-24 months, mature-node logic fabs are 6-12 months, polysilicon is 3-6 months). This inferential step is hidden in your domain expertise. When you code 30 episodes, you assign each a qualification-lag score (6 months, 12 months, etc.) based on end-market category. One researcher, no inter-coder check, no blind review. If two researchers coded the same 10 episodes, would they agree? You have not tested that. The ranking by qualification-lag will be robust if the variable is real and you coded it well, and fragile if you coded it via post-hoc rationalization.
issues.what_breaks: You present the ranking to the IC. An analyst asks: why is polysilicon rated 3-month lag? You say: 'industry standard for new supplier onboarding.' An aerospace analyst in the room says: 'actually, mid-program qualification in auto semis takes 12-18 months, not 6.' Your ranking shifts. You cannot defend it because the variable came from your head, not from data.
issues.fix: For each end-market category, cite a single published source (SEMI roadmap, customer disclosure, industry report) that documents qualification time. If none exists, admit the lag is inferred and report it as a hypothesis, not a fact. Consider running the analysis without ranking by qualification-lag, and instead simply asking: do episodes with known-long qualification times (aerospace, power semis) actually hold price while known-short ones (polysilicon, containers) do not? If the pattern emerges clearly, you have something. If you need to invoke qualification-lag as the explanation, you are retrofitting the story.

issues.summary: The plan lists 'pitfalls' (definitional drift, disclosure asymmetry, double-counting, etc.) but none of these are mitigated or tested; they are acknowledged and then ignored.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You note: 'disclosure asymmetry (signature announced, unwind silent) biasing toward durability; double-counting backlog/RPO/LTA value; prepayment as disguised financing funding the capacity ending the shortage.' These are real and serious. But then you do not say how you avoid them. How do you avoid double-counting when you use supplier 10-K disclosures, customer purchase-obligation tables, and customs shipment data all together? Which is the 'truth' when they disagree? You say 'shipment data wins' but that is a rule, not a solution — if shipment volume is high but customer 10-K obligation falls, did the customer truly exit the contract or just consume it? 'Disclosure asymmetry' means walks are silent; you will miss them. Your framework assumes you see all repricing; you will not. These are not pitfalls to list, they are reasons the analysis cannot reach the confidence it claims.
issues.what_breaks: You publish a finding: 'auto-semis LTAs repriced to near-spot within 3-4 quarters.' An investor asks: how do you know some customers did not quietly walk on their LTAs? Your answer: 'I would see it in customs data.' That is wrong; a customer who walks might buy at spot on the secondary market or from a different supplier, and you would not see an LTA walk in your data. You are confident you have seen repricing because you looked for repricing; you have not tested for undetected exits.
issues.fix: For the key question — whether repricing was complete or partial — name the specific check that would detect a silent walk. For auto semis, that might be: 'I check customer 10-K disclosures (Item 7) and compare year-on-year purchase obligations; a walk would show as a material reduction in reported obligations.' Then apply that check and report: 'X% of LTA value shows as repriced via disclosure, Y% as walked via obligation reduction, Z% indeterminate.' If Z is large, say so. Do not assume you have seen everything.

issues.summary: The plan will take 5-7 months to execute and will not produce a recommendation until the analysis is complete; an early kill signal is buried behind data assembly.
issues.why_it_applies_here: As proposed, the plan requires: (a) gathering and coding 20-30 contracts (8-10 weeks), (b) building a capacity ledger per market (6-8 weeks), (c) integrating price data (2 weeks), (d) running ranking analysis (2 weeks), (e) interpreting and stress-testing (3-4 weeks). The question that would kill the entire analysis early — 'do LTA repricing data exist in public disclosures in sufficient detail to validate the price-vs-volume split?' — comes in week 2-3 of the ranking analysis. If the answer is no, you have sunk 4 months. A cheaper first step would be: (1) pull 3-4 auto-semi customer 10-Ks and compare purchase obligations year-on-year, (2) pull 3-4 supplier 10-Ks and look for contract-liability movement, (3) check if that data is granular enough to track repricing. If it is not (which is likely), the whole analysis is infeasible, and you know that in 2 weeks instead of 18.
issues.what_breaks: You spend 18 weeks on the framework. In week 16, you discover that customer 10-K purchase-obligation tables roll up all suppliers and do not break out LTA repricing by counterparty. Your analysis cannot validate the price-split hypothesis. You have committed calendar and analyst time for no actionable result.
issues.fix: Start with a 1-week 'feasibility check': gather 5 auto-semi customer 10-Ks, 5 supplier 10-Ks, and 2-3 published price series, and manually verify whether the data granularity is sufficient to detect repricing at the customer level. If it is, proceed. If not, modify the approach to use only market-level data (aggregate capacity vs. aggregate LTA contracts) or admit the hypothesis cannot be tested with public data.

issues.summary: The plan produces a 'probability-weighted haircut, not a verdict,' but does not specify how this haircut is used or what counts as conviction.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You write: 'Output: a probability-weighted haircut, not a verdict, with a statement of what would justify the higher multiple.' A concentrated manager making a binary hold/buy/sell decision on one name does not use probability-weighted haircuts; they use narratives and conviction levels. What your IC will ask is: 'Should we own this name and if so at what price?' The plan's output will be: 'Shortage-era LTAs reprice to spot 60% of the time within 3-4 quarters if qualification-lag is below 12 months, 40% of the time if above; the company is aerospace-forward (high moat) so applies the second base rate; therefore the current multiple of 12x forward EBITDA should be discounted to 9x.' That is a narrative waiting to be built on top of the analysis, but the analysis does not build it. You have produced information for a model portfolio optimization system, not a memo for a partner to read.
issues.what_breaks: Your analyst hands in 25 pages of contract coding tables, qualification-lag rankings, and repricing base rates. The IC asks: 'What is the call?' The analyst says: 'It depends on the weighting of the moat variables.' The IC decides to table it and wait for a clearer picture. The analysis is correct but unactionable.
issues.fix: Add a final step: 'Apply base rates to this company.' Given that the target is aerospace-focused semis with disclosed LTA book of $X billion, what is the chance repricing is incomplete 8 quarters post-normalization? What price level does that imply? Build a 2-3 scenario table (moat holds, moat erodes slowly, moat erodes fast) and state which you believe given the contract language and customer mix. Connect the analysis to a position.

issues.summary: The plan is for answering the question 'Do shortage-era LTAs survive normalized supply?', but your company needs to answer 'Is this name worth buying at current price given LTA uncertainty?'. The plan is one input to the latter question, not the answer.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Your question from management is: 'Does that portend more customer long-term agreements and more durable revenue?' Your plan answers: 'Shortage-era LTAs are repriced 60-75% of the time within 3-4 quarters, and this case fits that pattern.' But the investment decision hinges on: what does the market already believe about repricing, what is priced into the stock, and what does management guidance imply about the numbers? If the market already discounts 70% repricing and the stock is down 20%, you do not need the analysis — you own it. If the market believes repricing will be minimal and the stock is near highs, the analysis is necessary. The plan does not place the finding in a valuation context. The plan also does not engage with what the seller of the stock believes — there is no articulation of who is on the other side of the trade, what they think LTA durability is, and why they are wrong.
issues.what_breaks: You publish the finding: 'LTAs will reprice 70% of the time based on qualification-lag analysis.' Management asks: 'So what is the right price-to-sales multiple?' You do not have an answer because the analysis does not bridge from repricing likelihood to valuation impact. You also do not know whether the stock already prices in 70% repricing, in which case the finding adds no value.
issues.fix: Preface the analysis with: 'Consensus view on LTA durability is [X%] based on [latest broker notes, management commentary]. We estimate repricing at [Y%] based on historical episodes. The valuation impact is [Z basis points of EV reduction] assuming [assumptions]. This argues for [conviction level] on [position].' Then run the episode analysis. Connect finding to decision.

issues.summary: The plan does not specify what 'supply normalization' means or when it has occurred, which is the event marker that triggers the observation window.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You define the event as 'first allocation-language filing, T=0,' and then measure repricing 'at T+4/8/12 quarters.' But you do not define when supply has normalized or when you start counting quarters. For polysilicon, is normalization when spot price fell to $100/kg (2011), or when it bottomed at $25/kg (2012), or when installed capacity stopped growing (2013)? For auto semis, is it when lead times fell below 6 months, or when customers stopped paying spot premia, or when new capacity came online? The T=0 marker (first allocation-language filing) is not the same as T=supply-normalized, and T+12 quarters from filing is not the same as T+12 quarters from normalization. If you misalign these dates, your repricing timeline is wrong.
issues.what_breaks: You code polysilicon: 'Filed allocation language in 2010, repriced by end-2012 (T+8 quarters).' But spot price was high through 2011 and did not fall until Q4 2011 and beyond. The customers might have repriced quickly after spot fell, but you are measuring from T=0=filing date, not T=0=spot-price start. You attribute repricing to qualification-lag when you are really measuring time-from-filing. The ranking by lag becomes noisy.
issues.fix: Define 'supply normalized' explicitly (spot price falls below X percentile of prior 2-year high, capacity exceeds demand by Y%, lead times fall to Z, etc.) and make that your T=0 marker. Or: acknowledge that filing date and normalization date diverge, and report repricing time relative to both. Or: use only cases where the two are close (HBM, where allocation language and spot-price movement are proximate).

issues.summary: The plan claims to test where the signal should NOT work, but does not pre-commit to which cases are negative controls or what result would falsify the ordering by qualification-lag.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You write: 'Test that aerospace/LNG score durable and MLCC/containers fragile, ordered by qualification lag not label.' This is good — you are naming negative controls. But you have not pre-committed: (a) which of the 20-30 episodes are intended as negative controls, (b) what counts as a 'pass' of the negative-control test, (c) what would happen if aerospace did NOT score durable, and (d) how you would adjust the hypothesis if LNG (highest-quality LTAs) repriced despite having a hard moat. If you wait until you see the data and then decide post-hoc which episodes are controls, you have not controlled for anything.
issues.what_breaks: You run the analysis and find: aerospace/semis held (as predicted), containers repriced (as predicted), MLCC repriced (as predicted), but LNG repriced at a lower rate than expected — is that a falsification of the qualification-lag hypothesis or an explanation for why LNG is special? You can rationalize either. You have not pre-committed to the threshold that would count as failure.
issues.fix: Before running the analysis, list the 20-30 episodes, mark each as either 'predicted to hold,' 'predicted to reprice,' or 'outcome uncertain,' with the qualification-lag reason for each prediction. Commit to a majority-vote rule: if 7 of 10 predicted-to-hold episodes actually hold, the hypothesis passes; if fewer than 6 do, it fails. Then run the data. Do not change the rule after seeing results.

issues.summary: The plan conflates 'shortage-era LTAs' (what customers want during tight supply) with 'LTAs that hold post-supply normalization' (what the investment thesis requires), without testing whether the population is the same.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Not all customers sign LTAs during shortage; some wait for spot. Of those who sign, not all are binding. Of those that are binding, the customers most likely to walk are the ones that signed at the worst terms. You are sampling on the LTA signings that happened (selection bias) and then asking whether those survived. The LTA book at the company today is the LTA book that was signed during the shortage; the repricing/walking you observe is on that population. But the question is: do shortage-era LTAs as a category survive? To answer that, you need to know what fraction of customers signed LTAs during shortage, and of those, what fraction's LTAs survive. The plan does not measure the numerator — it assumes all customers signed and measures repricing on the denominator.
issues.what_breaks: You observe: '70% of disclosed auto-semi LTAs repriced within 3-4 quarters.' This sounds durable. But if only 40% of auto-customers signed shortage-era LTAs at all, the durability rate of shortage-era LTAs in the customer base is 70% * 40% = 28%, not 70%. The finding is correct for the LTAs that were signed, but misleading for the cohort of shortage-era arrangements.
issues.fix: Pull customer disclosures and estimate: what fraction of purchase commitments were LTA vs. spot during the shortage period? For the company in question, what fraction of revenue is from signed LTAs today? If LTA book is only 20% of revenue, even complete repricing does not save the growth case. State the denominator.

issues.summary: Executed as proposed, the plan will not be defensible to an experienced investor or IC member because the key inferences (qualification-lag, hidden capacity, repricing magnitude) are not separable from post-hoc storytelling.
issues.why_it_applies_here: An IC member from a technical background (an engineer, a former operator, a quant) will ask: 'Show me the contract for Infineon and a specific customer where you classified it as repriced. Show me the math.' You will pull the 10-K and the contract-liability note, and show a $200M write-down. The IC member will ask: 'How do you know the $200M was repriced and not volume-walkback? What contract language tells you that?' You will say: 'I looked at guidance and shipment trends and inferred repricing.' The member will lose confidence because the connection between the contract and the conclusion is broken. You need to show 1-2 worked examples, traced end-to-end, where you have the actual contract language, the repricing terms, and the post-normalization outcome. Without that, the framework is a black box.
issues.what_breaks: You present the analysis. An IC member asks you to pick one episode and walk her through it: polysilicon, Hemlock, pick one customer case and show the contract and the repricing. You pull Hemlock vs. SolarWorld and realize the litigation files do not give you the actual renegotiated price terms — they give you claim and counter-claim. You cannot show the before/after contract. The IC member concludes you have not actually validated the repricing hypothesis on a single named deal.
issues.fix: Run the analysis on only the cases where you have the full contract, or where the repricing terms are public (litigation outcome, settlement disclosures, customer/supplier joint announcements). For auto semis, find 1-2 cases where Renesas/Wolfspeed or Infineon/customer posted joint statements on repricing. Trace those end-to-end. Present those as the core evidence. Use the broader episode set to estimate base rates, but ground the framework in 2-3 cases your IC can verify themselves by reading the same documents.

issues.summary: The plan is silent on whether there is actually an edge to this analysis — what the market currently believes about LTA durability and where this finding diverges from consensus.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You write: 'Large disclosed LTA book is a coincident indicator of cycle peak, not durability — prepayments funding the book fund the capacity that destroys the pricing.' This is a variant view (consensus believes LTA book supports multiple expansion). But you do not establish consensus explicitly. What do the latest broker notes say about LTA durability? What does management guidance imply? If three of four semiconductor brokers already think 'LTAs will reprice due to qualification-lag dynamics,' then your analysis confirms consensus and produces no edge. If none of them have written that, you may have a variant view. The plan does not do this comparison.
issues.what_breaks: You deliver the finding. Your PM checks the latest Citi/Morgan Stanley/Goldman semicond notes. All three say something close to: 'LTA durability is uncertain; repricing risk is material.' Your finding is consensus-confirming. The stock has already priced it in. You have no edge.
issues.fix: Start by explicitly stating what you believe sell-side consensus is on LTA repricing ('consensus believes LTA book is durable 75%+' or 'consensus is agnostic'). State what you will conclude from the analysis that would differ from that consensus. Then run the analysis. If your conclusion aligns with consensus, say so and explain why the stock is still attractively priced despite that; do not position the analysis as new information.

issues.summary: The plan will require specialized data feeds (TrendForce, Fastmarkets, UxC, Xeneta, Drewry, Panjiva, ImportGenius) that are expensive, may have limited history, and introduce vendor risk and licensing complexity.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Your firm does not maintain a data-infrastructure team. Licensing 6+ specialized commodity feeds introduces a dependency on vendors, procurement, and legal review of the terms. Some of these feeds (TrendForce, Fastmarkets) require subscriptions and have limited historical backfill. Some (Panjiva, ImportGenius) are expensive and may require API integration your firm cannot support. If you license them for a one-time analysis and then an IC member wants to check the analysis a year later, the license may have lapsed. If you license them ongoing as part of the framework, the cost carries regardless of whether you run the analysis again.
issues.what_breaks: You license TrendForce and Fastmarkets for $50K/year. The analysis runs over 6 months and concludes. Next year, no one asks the question again, but the licenses renew. You have a $50K annual cost for an analysis run once.
issues.fix: Start with free or widely-available price data (spot prices from public exchanges, broker research reports, indices like LBMA, ICE, NYMEX where commodity prices are published). Use those first. Only if the analysis *requires* specialist feeds (HBM pricing, for example, which is not public) and you have committed to an HBM-focused scope, license the feed. Do not commit to a 6-feed infrastructure before the analysis proves it is necessary.

issues.summary: The plan is sophisticated and impressive, but solves a research problem for a large systematic firm, not an actionable problem for a concentrated fundamental manager.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A quant firm with 50+ researchers, a data team, and a model portfolio would ask: 'Do shortage-era LTAs have a different repricing distribution than other contracts? Can we trade this systematically across 100+ suppliers?' This plan answers that. A concentrated long-only manager with $400M AUM and 25-30 names would ask: 'Is this particular company worth buying at this price given LTA risk?' The plan does not answer that. It produces a generalizable framework when what you need is depth on one business decision.
issues.what_breaks: You spend 6 months building a framework that shows 'LTAs reprice 70% of the time in semis but only 30% of the time in HBM due to qualification lag.' The IC takes a breath and asks: 'And what is the stock worth?' You do not have an answer because you have not valued the company under your 70% repricing scenario vs. the 30% scenario. You have written a research paper, not a memo.
issues.fix: Scope the work to one company. Use the repricing framework as a model input, not the output. Work backward from valuation: 'If we assume 70% repricing in years 2-3, what does that imply for revenue and margin? At that number, what is the fair value? Is the stock now attractive?' That is a call the IC can act on.

issues.summary: The plan includes live HBM pre-registration, but the pre-registration does not specify the falsification criteria tightly enough to prevent rationalization when results arrive.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You write: 'For the live HBM case, pre-register 3-5 falsifiable checks (contract-liability direction, RPO growth threshold, customs shipment tracking, customer 10-K obligation-table increase), each checkable within 12 months.' But you have not stated what level of contract-liability movement counts as falsifying the hypothesis, what RPO growth rate, what customs volume threshold. 'RPO growth threshold' — growing or shrinking? By what %? If RPO grows 20%, is repricing incomplete or complete? You cannot answer yet, which means you will decide when you see the data.
issues.what_breaks: HBM data arrives. SK Hynix contract-liability fell 30% (repricing), but RPO grew (customers are still committed). Did repricing happen or not? You have two signals pointing opposite ways. You write: 'Contract-liability moved as predicted; RPO growth reflects new customers added, not LTA durability.' You have explained away the contradiction without having pre-committed to it.
issues.fix: Before 2025, publish: 'We will check HBM repricing by measuring [single metric — customer 10-K obligation table reduction, yes-or-no]. If customer obligations fall 25%+ year-on-year, repricing is confirmed. If customer obligations stay flat or grow, repricing is not confirmed. Either outcome is falsifiable; we will not cherry-pick among RPO, contract-liability, and custom data.'

issues.summary: The plan will consume 6-7 months of calendar and analyst time on a research question that may already be priced, may have a clear answer from broker notes, and may not move the needle on a single-name decision.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Your firm has 2 PMs and 2 analysts for $400M in 25-30 names. Consuming 50%+ of one analyst's time for 6+ months on a cross-market study of LTA repricing is a high opportunity cost. The question might be answerable in 2 weeks of reading (earnings calls, broker notes, customer disclosures, one price series) plus 2 weeks of sketch modeling (what does repricing mean for revenue and margin). If that 4-week version shows the hypothesis is already confirmed by recent commentary, the 6-month version is waste.
issues.what_breaks: Your analyst does week 1 of the plan and reads 10 recent broker notes on semis. Nine of them say: 'LTA repricing likely but not uniform — depends on customer qualification difficulty.' Your hypothesis is already out there. You have 5 more months of work ahead to prove something consensus already mostly believes.
issues.fix: Before committing the analyst to the multi-month framework, run a 2-week preliminary: read latest broker notes, earnings-call transcripts, and customer disclosures. Check if the answer is already consensus. If 3+ brokers have already made the qualification-lag argument, declare the idea un-investable (no edge) and move on. If none have, then build the framework.

issues.summary: The plan's specification of 'base rates by feature' requires coding by feature, but features will not be independent (qualification-lag and sourcing and credit are often correlated), making the feature-by-feature ranking susceptible to confounding.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You write: 'compute unconditional and conditional base rates by feature (qualification lag, sourcing, credit, pricing), ranked not regressed.' Feature coding is valuable, but when features are not independent, a ranking by one feature can mask the true driver. Aerospace programs (high qualification-lag) usually have strong customer credit and high-value customers; polysilicon (low qualification-lag) has weak customer credit and commodity pricing. When you rank by qualification-lag and find aerospace holds, you cannot tell if it is the lag or the customer quality or the pricing structure. Regression is usually the answer, but you said 'ranked not regressed' — which suggests you are avoiding regression to keep the method simple. That simplicity has a cost: the ranking will confound variables.
issues.what_breaks: You find: aerospace/HBM hold (high qualification-lag); polysilicon/containers repriced (low lag). This looks like a qualification-lag story. But aerospace also has premium customers and take-or-pay language, while polysilicon has commodity-trading buyers and flex bands. You have not separated qualification-lag from contract language from customer credit. The ranking by lag might be spurious.
issues.fix: You cannot avoid the confounding without multivariate analysis. Either: (a) use regression or stratified comparison within matched pairs (e.g., two semis cases with similar lag but different customer credit, and see which holds), or (b) acknowledge that the ranking is univariate and confounding is possible, and present it as 'correlation, not causation.' Report the caveat.

issues.summary: The plan does not specify what level of conviction or haircut the IC should take from a successful validation of the LTA repricing hypothesis for the company in question.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You write: 'Output: a probability-weighted haircut, not a verdict.' If the analysis validates the hypothesis (LTAs will reprice 70% of the time), what does the company's stock deserve as a discount to the base case (case where all LTAs hold)? Is it a 5% EV reduction? 20%? Is that certainty high enough to short or high enough to trim an existing position, or only high enough to be cautious? Without connecting the repricing probability to a valuation impact and a conviction level, the output is a statistical finding without a decision input.
issues.what_breaks: Your analyst finishes the analysis and reports: 'LTAs will reprice 65-70% of the time based on historical base rates.' The IC asks: 'So the stock is worth $X less, yes?' The analyst says: 'Depends on how much of revenue is LTA book and the price elasticity of volumes.' The IC realizes the research does not answer the valuation question.
issues.fix: Add a final reconciliation step: 'Repricing assumptions imply [Y]% reduction in out-year revenue. Margin impact is [Z]%. Fair value under repricing scenario is $[A] vs. $[B] under hold scenario. Current price is $[C]. Position is [long/short/hold] with conviction [%].' Connect the probability to the price target.

issues.summary: The plan lacks an explicit statement of what the company has disclosed about LTA mix, pricing, and customer concentration, which is the ground truth the analysis should build on.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Before building a cross-market base rate, you need to characterize this company's specific LTA book: What % of revenue is LTA vs. spot? What % of LTA volume is aerospace (high moat) vs. commodity (low moat)? What is the disclosed contract repricing/termination risk? The company's 10-K and earnings calls should answer most of this. The plan assumes you will use this data to 'apply base rates to the company,' but the plan does not specify that you will extract and organize this baseline information first. If the company discloses that 90% of LTA revenue is aerospace-qualified semis, the repricing risk is much lower than the 70% base rate. If 70% is commodity polysilicon-like, risk is higher.
issues.what_breaks: You run the repricing analysis and find 70% of LTAs reprice within 3-4 quarters. You tell management: 'This company's LTAs will likely reprice.' Management asks: 'But our LTA book is 80% aerospace semis and 20% polysilicon. Do your base rates even apply?' You realize you did not segment the company's actual LTA mix, and the base rate is useless.
issues.fix: Before running the episode analysis, do a data pull: extract from this company's last 3 10-Ks and 8 earnings call transcripts: (a) total LTA revenue and mix by end-market, (b) contract repricing language if disclosed, (c) customer concentration within LTA book, (d) management guidance on LTA durability. Organize this as a baseline case. Then ask: do the historical base rates apply to this mix? The analysis now answers the company question, not the general question.

issues.summary: The plan conflates 'repricing' (contract terms change) with 'price realization decline' (customer pays less), when the two can be separated (customer accepts lower volume at original price, or lower price at original volume).
issues.why_it_applies_here: A customer can 'reprice' a contract by accepting allocation cuts. An LTA that promised 100 units/quarter at $10/unit can be 'repriced' to 60 units/quarter at $10/unit, delivering $600 per quarter instead of $1000. In the financials, that looks like volume loss, not price loss. Your customs data will show lower shipments. Your price feeds will show flat prices. Your contract-liability note will show a write-down (lower future PV of the contract). When you analyze repricing, can you tell the difference between: (a) customer pays $6/unit for 100 units, and (b) customer pays $10/unit for 60 units? Both reduce value 40%. Only (a) is price repricing; (b) is volume repricing. The plan does not clearly separate them.
issues.what_breaks: You code auto semis as 'repriced 80% of volume.' Management asks: 'Repriced meaning price fell, or volume was cut?' You answer: 'Primarily volume allocation cuts.' Management says: 'So we still get $10/unit, we just make less stuff?' You respond: 'Correct.' Management realizes the pricing model survived; it is the capacity utilization that fell. Your repricing narrative has broken down because repricing and volume cuts have opposite implications for gross margin.
issues.fix: When coding repricing, separate it into: (a) price-down repricing ($/unit falls), (b) volume-down repricing (units/period falls), (c) mixed. For each episode, report the split. State whether the plan is about price durability ($/unit) or revenue durability ($/unit * units). The two are different stories.

issues.summary: The plan is missing an explicit comparison to the null hypothesis: if I do nothing and just trust management guidance, how much repricing risk is already baked into my view?
issues.why_it_applies_here: Every management team in a cyclical industry knows that long-term contracts reprice. Your company's management has already guided you through a supply cycle or multiple cycles. When they say 'we expect LTA durability through 2025,' they have presumably thought about the repricing risk and are claiming it is low. The cross-market analysis finds 70% repricing. Is that worse than management's guidance, or consistent with it? Without this comparison, you have built a framework that may be proving something the company has already disclosed.
issues.what_breaks: Your analysis concludes: 'LTAs will likely reprice to near-spot.' You note this on the IC memo. The IC reads the company's latest 10-K and finds management says: 'We have confidence in our long-term customer relationships and expect demand to remain strong even as supply normalizes.' The IC interprets this as management already pricing in some repricing risk. Your analysis is not news.
issues.fix: Include in the memo: 'Management's latest guidance implies [X% repricing risk implied in the numbers]. Historical base rates across 20+ episodes suggest [Y% repricing risk]. Our central view is [Z%]. This [exceeds / aligns with / falls short of] management's disclosed view.' That shows whether the analysis changes the consensus.

issues.summary: The plan names 'definitional drift across LTA types' as a pitfall but does not mitigate it — the analysis will code a take-or-pay contract and a reservation contract in the same ranking, conflating their repricing dynamics.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Take-or-pay contracts (customer pays whether it takes or not) reprice differently than reservation contracts (customer reserves capacity but pays only if it takes). A take-or-pay that reprices usually reprices downward (customer pushes back); a reservation that reprices might reprice upward (supplier charges a reservation fee). Your coding will lump these together as 'LTA.' When you rank by qualification-lag, you are mixing a contract type that is very sticky (take-or-pay, aerospace) with a contract type that is very flexible (reservation, semis). You list this as a pitfall but do not fix it.
issues.what_breaks: You code aerospace power semis: 'take-or-pay, reprices downward 30% of the time.' You code memory semis: 'reservation, reprices downward 85% of the time.' You rank both by qualification-lag and find aerospace is more durable. But the difference might be take-or-pay vs. reservation, not qualification-lag. You have confounded contract type with product category.
issues.fix: Stratify the analysis by contract type first: separate take-or-pay from reservations from other terms, and rank within each stratum by qualification-lag. Report results by stratum. This ensures you are comparing apples to apples.

issues.summary: The plan claims to rely on 'shipment data wins' as the truth over disclosure, but customs data is 12-16 weeks delayed and may not separate LTA shipments from spot market shipments.
issues.why_it_applies_here: You write: 'Reconcile supplier, customer, and shipment data; where they disagree, shipment data wins.' Shipment data from Panjiva or ImportGenius is derived from bills of lading and customs records, which are public but delayed. More importantly, shipment data does not tell you the contract status: a shipment might satisfy an LTA or be a new spot purchase. If a customer is repricing an LTA and filling the gap with spot purchases, your shipment data will show total volume (LTA + spot) and price weighted across both. You cannot separate them without the customer's internal allocation, which you do not have. You are assuming shipment data is clean and unambiguous; it is not.
issues.what_breaks: A customer (TSMC, Samsung) has an LTA with a supplier for 80 units/month at $10/unit. As prices fall, the customer reprices the LTA to 60 units/month at $8/unit. The customer buys the other 20 units/month at spot price $6/unit. Your shipment data shows 80 units/month at a blended $9/unit. Your price feed shows spot at $6/unit. You infer 'repricing incomplete,' when in fact repricing was complete (LTA repriced to $8) plus market purchase at $6.
issues.fix: Acknowledge that shipment data reconciles volume, not price composition. Do not use it as the arbiter of repricing. Instead, use it to check: is shipment volume consistent with contract-liability movement? If contract-liability falls 30% but shipment volume is flat, repricing might be price-only or might be inferred incorrectly. Flag the inconsistency as a sign you need the actual contract terms. For the live HBM test, commit to a single truth source (customer 10-K obligation table, yes-or-no) rather than trying to triangulate.

issues.summary: The plan assumes that all 'shortage-era' contracts can be lumped together despite orders-of-magnitude differences in their underlying supply elasticity — a shortage lasting 2 years (auto semis 2021-2023) is not the same as one lasting 8 years (polysilicon 2007-2015).
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan uses 'shortage-era LTA' as a category encompassing polysilicon 2007-2012, auto semis 2021-2023, HBM 2023-2026. The duration of shortage is very different, and repricing dynamics depend on it. A brief shock (auto semis, 2 years) creates repricing pressure quickly once supply catches up. A chronic shortage (polysilicon, 8 years) allows long-term contracts to age and the repricing problem to be diluted by new contracts written at lower prices. When you pool repricing rates across shortages of different duration, you are averaging apples (2-year shortage) and oranges (8-year shortage) and calling it a finding.
issues.what_breaks: You compute repricing rate across 20 episodes and find 70%. But auto semis repriced at 85% within 2 years (because supply came back fast), while polysilicon repriced at 55% within 8 years (because shortage was long and supply came back slowly). You are mixing shortage durations and producing a blended rate that applies to none of them. If HBM shortage is predicted to last 3-4 years (like auto semis), the 55% rate from polysilicon is the wrong base rate.
issues.fix: Stratify by shortage duration: separate episodes where supply normalized within 18 months (auto semis) from those where it took 3+ years (polysilicon, uranium). Compute base rates within each stratum. For HBM, estimate how long the shortage is expected to persist (per SEMI, foundry guidance, capex plans) and apply the matching stratum's repricing rate. Or: admit you cannot handle shortage duration heterogeneity and confine the analysis to the subset with similar durations.

issues.summary: The plan does not address whether repricing is endogenous to the company's actions — a supplier that makes repricing difficult (takes customers to court, refuses spot sales, enforces take-or-pay) will see different repricing rates than one that accommodates it, and the difference is not about the market, it is about the firm's bargaining power.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Repricing rates vary by company skill and negotiating power, not just by market structure. Renesas accommodated repricing requests; Hemlock litigated. One will show high repricing rates in your data, the other low. You are ranking by 'qualification-lag' when half the variance might be 'how hard does the company fight to keep the price?' This is a company-specific variable, not a market variable, and it will not generalize to your company unless you know its bargaining posture. The plan does not address this.
issues.what_breaks: You find that Hemlock's LTAs held price because qualification-lag was high (correct) and it was a litigious company (not stated). Your company is also a qualified supplier but is known as customer-friendly and accommodating. You apply the 'held' base rate from Hemlock and overestimate repricing resistance. Your company's repricing rate is higher because of its own negotiating style, not because the market is different.
issues.fix: For each episode, note the supplier's known reputation and behavior: does it litigate, accommodate, or split the difference? Build a small table showing repricing rates by (qualification-lag, company-type). State that your company's repricing rate depends on its own negotiating posture, which is a variable the analysis cannot capture. If your company is customer-friendly, add a 10-15% repricing uplift to the base rate.

issues.summary: The plan does not discuss whether management has already disclosed LTA risk or negotiated repricing during the cycle, which would mean the risk is known and priced rather than hidden.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The company you are analyzing has already been through one quarter or two of supply normalization (as of late 2024). Management has likely already discussed LTA repricing risk on earnings calls. The stock price may already reflect market belief that repricing is happening. Your analysis, even if correct, may be confirming what is already known and priced. Without checking management commentary and recent analyst notes, you do not know if the finding is news or consensus.
issues.what_breaks: Your analysis concludes: repricing risk is 70%. You present this to the IC. The IC notes that the stock is down 25% from highs and cites two broker notes from October 2024 calling out repricing risk. The analysis has confirmed something three months of market repricing has already priced in.
issues.fix: Pull the last 2 quarters of earnings transcripts and 3-4 recent broker notes. Summarize: what is management saying about repricing? What is consensus saying? Does your 70% estimate exceed, match, or underestimate the market view? If it matches, the stock is fairly priced for repricing. If it exceeds, you may have a short idea. If it falls short, you may have a long idea. State the comparison explicitly.

issues.summary: The plan lacks a simple reasonableness check on its central claim: if 70% of shortage-era LTAs reprice, why didn't the market price in repricing risk faster and more deeply as supply normalized?
issues.why_it_applies_here: If repricing is a 70% base-rate phenomenon, it should be common knowledge. As supply normalized in auto semis (late 2022-2023), customers started walking and repricing. Smart portfolio managers would have seen it happening in real time. The stock prices of suppliers like Infineon and NXP fell 30-40% in 2022-2023 largely on growth and margin repricing concerns. If the market knew repricing was coming, why was the repricing surprise priced in gradually rather than all at once? This suggests either: (a) repricing was not as obvious as 70% would suggest, (b) the market knew but did not care (repricing was already in guidance), or (c) other factors (macro, growth) dominated repricing in the stock move. The plan does not engage with why the market lagged the repricing signal.
issues.what_breaks: You present your 70% repricing finding as news. Your PM asks: 'If repricing is this common, why wasn't it priced in faster in auto semis?' You do not have a good answer because you have not engaged with the market's repricing speed and the stock's repricing move. The finding might be correct but not incremental.
issues.fix: Overlay the repricing rate on the stock price performance during each episode. For auto semis, plot: (a) the stock price, (b) the month repricing became obvious, (c) the month repricing became public. If the stock fell immediately, the repricing was priced fast and your analysis is confirmatory. If the stock lagged repricing, you have a story about market efficiency. Explain the lag. State whether your advantage is speed (you see repricing before the market) or insight (you estimate the repricing rate better than the market), or neither.

issues.summary: The plan's output is ordered by psychological plausibility rather than by disconfirming-power: qualification-lag is the first hypothesis tested, but 'hidden capacity' or 'disclosure asymmetry' would kill it faster if they are real.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The kill-first principle says: run the test that would disprove the hypothesis if it applies, before the confirmation test. The plan tests qualification-lag first (finding aerospace holds, polysilicon reprices, fitting the hypothesis). But if disclosure asymmetry is real — if quiet repricing walks are common and do not show up in public data — then the entire ranking is biased and the hypothesis unfalsifiable. A cheaper first step would be: audit whether your repricing detection (via contract-liability, customer obligations, customs data) is complete or systematically missing silent walks. If silent walks are >20% of the total repricing, your ranking is noise.
issues.what_breaks: You rank by qualification-lag and find a clean separation (aerospace holds, polysilicon reprices). You present this to the IC. The IC asks: 'How do you know you are not missing silent walks in the high-lag cases, which would bias the ranking?' You realize you have not tested whether your detection method is complete. The entire ranking might be an artifact of disclosure asymmetry, not qualification-lag.
issues.fix: Before ranking, run a sensitivity check: assume silent walks are [10%, 25%, 50%] of total repricing, uniformly distributed across all episodes. Re-compute ranking. Does qualification-lag still separate aerospace from polysilicon, or does the ranking collapse? If it collapses, admission-of-detection-incompleteness is a blocker and the ranking is unfalsifiable. If it holds, you have defended against the disclosure-asymmetry objection. Report the sensitivity result.

issues.summary: The plan will take 6+ months and will not produce a recommendation the company can act on within a reasonable decision-making timeline.
issues.why_it_applies_here: Supply normalization in semiconductors is happening now (late 2024, into 2025). Customer repricing is happening now. The company is guiding on LTA durability now. By the time your analyst finishes a 6-month cross-market study in mid-2025, the repricing in this particular company will be largely visible in the 2024 and 2025 financials. The analysis will be retrospective, not predictive. For a single-name call, you need an answer in 4-6 weeks, not 6 months.
issues.what_breaks: You finish the analysis in June 2025. The company has reported 2024 results (Jan 2025) and Q1 2025 results (May 2025). Management has already been asked on earnings calls about repricing and given guidance on 2025 margins. The repricing you were analyzing is already public. Your analysis is confirming what is already known.
issues.fix: Run a 4-week version: read earnings transcripts, broker notes, and customer disclosures, model repricing impact on 2025-2026 numbers, make a call.
